question: How does destructuring work for objects and arrays?
shortAnswer: Destructuring unpacks values from objects or arrays into variables using a pattern that mirrors the structure: { a, b } = obj picks properties by name, [x, y] = arr picks items by position.
explanation: Object destructuring matches property names, so order doesn't matter, and you can rename ({ name: userName }) or provide defaults ({ age = 18 }). Nested patterns reach into inner structures in one line. Array destructuring works positionally, supports skipping holes ([a, , c]) and defaults, and its rest element collects the tail. The swap idiom [a, b] = [b, a] falls out naturally. In function signatures, destructured parameters give named options with defaults — the pattern behind most modern APIs (e.g., fetch options). Combined with spread it handles immutable updates: ({ ...user, name: 'New' }) clones while overriding. Common uses: pulling data out of API responses, iterating Object.entries, and cleaning up props in React components.
interviewTip: Show renaming, defaults and nesting in one compact example — three features in five lines reads as fluency rather than memorization.
commonMistakes: Misremembering that arrays destructure by key — they use position.
Forgetting parentheses when destructuring to existing variables: ({a} = obj);

question: What is the difference between shallow and deep copies, and how do you create each?
shortAnswer: A shallow copy duplicates only the top level — nested objects are still shared references. A deep copy duplicates every level so nothing is shared. Spread/Object.assign are shallow; structuredClone is deep.
explanation: Objects live on the heap and variables hold references, so assignment never copies. Spread ({ ...obj }) and Object.assign() create new top-level containers, but any nested object/array is copied as a pointer — mutating nestedObj.x through either version affects both. Deep copying historically meant JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)), which loses functions, undefined, Dates, Maps/Sets and throws on circular refs. Modern JavaScript ships structuredClone(), which handles all built-in types and cycles correctly (but still not functions). Libraries like Lodash's cloneDeep remain common in older codebases. Choosing depth is a real design decision: shallow copies are cheap and usually right for state updates where you replace nested levels wholesale; deep copies protect against untrusted or deeply mutated input at higher cost.
interviewTip: Demonstrate the shared-reference bug first — it proves you understand *why* — then present structuredClone as the modern answer and note JSON's pitfalls.
commonMistakes: Believing spread performs a deep copy.
Recommending JSON round-trip without mentioning Date/undefined loss.

question: When would you choose map, filter, and reduce?
shortAnswer: map transforms every item into a new array of the same length, filter keeps items matching a predicate, and reduce folds everything into a single value — sum, object, anything.
explanation: These three cover most array processing. map answers 'transform each element': same length in and out. filter answers 'which elements do I keep?': length shrinks, elements unchanged. reduce is the general-purpose folder: it accumulates a result across iterations — numbers (totals), objects (grouping/counting), even new arrays when chaining feels wasteful. They're chainable because each returns a fresh array/value, leaving the original untouched — important for predictable code and immutable state updates. Performance note: many chained passes can be merged into one reduce if profiling shows it matters, but clarity wins by default. Knowing forEach exists too helps articulate the difference: forEach returns undefined and is for side effects, not transformation.
interviewTip: Anchor each method to one verb — transform, select, fold — then run a realistic pipeline. Mentioning forEach's side-effect-only role shows completeness.
commonMistakes: Using map for side effects instead of forEach.
Forgetting the initial value argument of reduce, causing crashes on empty arrays.
